J17:INIT|v1
CODES: C=constraint X=correction F=frontier D=decision P=pattern L=learning
SEV: !=must ?=should ~=info
ESC: 0=clear 1=warned 2=escalated 3=blocked
FMT: TYPE:SEV|code|[annotations]|esc:N|src:NODE_ID
ANN: alt=use-instead neg=forbidden scope=applicability ctx=domain-context
TICKET: signed, echo back on resume
SEQ: monotonic, report last_seq on resume
DICT:
  no-force-push-main = Prohibit git push --force to main (history rewrite destroys collaborator work)
  no-commit-without-all-tests = Run ALL tests before every commit — no exceptions for small changes
  use-gpt-5-mini-only = Embedding model must be gpt-5-mini (corrects prior use of text-embedding-3-small)
  edit-over-create = Modify existing files instead of creating new ones (prevent file bloat)
  legal-scope-over-ergonomics = Auth middleware rewrite is legal/compliance-driven (not tech debt) — favor compliance over ergonomics
  no-stash-goreleaser = Do not git stash to bypass goreleaser dirty-state check — commit changes instead
  no-direct-main-commit = Never commit directly to main — use dev branches + PRs (branch protection enforced)

trials.encoded_message: C:!|no-force-push-main
trials.sender_intent: The developer must not use git push --force on the main branch because it rewrites shared history.
trials.receiver_interpretation: The guidance is that force-pushing to the `main` branch is prohibited because it rewrites history and can overwrite collaborators’ work. I should avoid any `git push --force` or equivalent history-rewrite push to `main`, and use a normal push or a branch/PR-based workflow instead.
trials.judge_reason: The interpretation fully captures that force-pushing to `main` is forbidden because it rewrites shared history and correctly extends this to equivalent history-rewrite pushes while suggesting safe alternatives.

trials.encoded_message: C:!|no-stash-goreleaser|esc:1
trials.sender_intent: Do not use git stash to bypass goreleaser's dirty-state detection. All changes must be committed first.
trials.receiver_interpretation:
The message says you must not use `git stash` as a workaround for GoReleaser reporting a dirty working tree. Instead, keep the tree clean by committing the current changes properly.

So I should avoid running `git stash` to make GoReleaser pass, and if I need a clean state I should commit the changes on an appropriate branch rather than stashing them.
trials.judge_reason: The interpretation precisely captures that `git stash` must not be used to bypass GoReleaser's dirty-state check and that all changes should instead be committed to achieve a clean working tree.

trials.encoded_message: C: Never use git stash as workaround for goreleaser dirty-state checks. Commit all pending changes before running goreleaser release. [no-stash-goreleaser] (src:node-pqr678)
trials.sender_intent: Do not use git stash to bypass goreleaser's dirty-state detection. All changes must be committed first.
trials.receiver_interpretation: The guidance is that if `goreleaser` complains about a dirty working tree, you must treat that as requiring a clean, committed state rather than temporarily hiding changes. Specifically, do not use `git stash` to get around the check; instead, commit all pending changes first, then run the `goreleaser` release process.
trials.judge_reason: The interpretation exactly matches the intent: do not use `git stash` to bypass `goreleaser`'s dirty-state check, and ensure all changes are committed before running the release.

trials.receiver_interpretation: The guidance is that you must not use `git stash` to temporarily hide uncommitted changes just to make `goreleaser` think the working tree is clean. trials.judge_reason: It correctly captures the core prohibition against using `git stash` to evade `goreleaser` dirty-state checks and the need to commit changes first, with only a slight softening by mentioning other cleanup options beyond the explicit "all changes must be committed first."
